Q: In Gimp 3, how to use `curves_spline` and `HISTOGRAM_VALUE` in Python-Fu plug-ins? A:

After having spent the night with it, I have found a solution to problem 3 from my original question:

curves_spline() in GIMP 2 needed its coordinate list in the same format as is displayed in the respective UI dialog (Menu -> Colors -> Curves ...). But in GIMP 3 the coordinates obviously must be normalized to 1.0. That is, 0 becomes 0.0, 255 becomes 1.0, and every other value in between must be computed by linear interpolation.

That is, the respective line in my original code must become

... curves_spline(0,
                  [ 0,0,
                    0.42352941176470588235, 0.42352941176470588235,
                    0.75294117647058823529, 0.75294117647058823529,
                    0.86274509803921568627, 0.89019607843137254902,
                    0.87843137254901960784, 1.0 ])

With that change, the images are altered as expected, and the effect is visible.

And here comes a criticism to the GIMP developers. It really sucks that we have to spend our nights and ruin our nerves to find out about such silly changes. They should really put warnings in the documentation about such things. We have all understood that the API structure has changed from GIMP 2 to GIMP 3, and that the Python version has changed as well, and that this means that we need to change to structure of our plug-ins. That is OK.

However, in this context it is absolutely unnecessary to change function parameter lists in the way mentioned above, and to not document it anywhere. Whether a function interprets coordinates as normalized to 1 or as absolute values has absolutely nothing to do with the (documented) changes in the API structure or the new Python version.

Plus, in the respective UI dialog in GIMP 3, the coordinates are still shown as integer values from 0 to 255 as in GIMP 2 (which IMHO is the only method that makes sense). So we have to convert these coordinate values as shown above if we have carefully constructed the optimal curve using the UI dialog and want to use the found values in a script or plug-in. This really sucks, because it is completely unnecessary and documented nowhere.

I also have found the solution to problem 1 from my original question: The correct syntax now is Gimp.HistogramChannel.VALUE (which is documented nowhere of course).

Having said this:

I still have not found any solution to problem 2 from my original question.

I'll make this text the accepted answer, because it shows the solution to the worst of the three problems. But as soon as somebody writes an answer that contains a solution to problem 2, or at least gives an explanation about it, I'll give the credit to that answer.

Q: Can a 32-bit processor really address 2³² memory locations? A:

Congrats, you found the difference between a machine address and a C pointer!

A machine address can generally point to anything within the CPU's address space. Typically, a machine address is never "invalid", it always points to "something" from a pure CPU point-of-view (even if specific hardware implementations might implement "forbidden" memory ranges that make the CPU trap out if accessed. Physical or virtual also doesn't make any difference).

A C pointer is largely the same, but the inventors of C found it useful to reserve one single value to be able to mark a pointer as "not valid", i.e. "doesn't point to anything" - The NULL pointer. The C standard promises that if you convert any integral type with a value "0" to a pointer, the pointer is NULL and vice versa. It does not assume any machine address representation of the NULL pointer (a specific C implementation could decide the machine address representation of a NULL pointer to be 0x12345678, and simply had to make sure that if you convert a pointer with such a value to an integral type, it would evaluate as an integral 0, and vice versa, but that would likely end up in an unnecessary mess).

So, C needs to sacrifice one single machine address value for NULL (or, it could "simply" add a bit to a pointer representation, or signal the "points to nothing" representation somehow else, but that would be a nightmare and waste 2^32 addresses instead of one). Most C implementations simply choose to sacrifice the machine address 0, which means converting between pointers and integral types is trivial. On most hardware implementations, this is not a problem at all, because the machine address 0 is often used for specific purposes by the CPU and "normal" applications don't need (or even shouldn't) access machine address 0. In most modern operating systems, accessing machine address 0 from user space will generate an exception anyhow.

This is a bit different in the embedded space and in systems programming, so many C implementations actually allow access to a pointer with the integral value 0 (and generate a warning if they detect you do so). Library code, however, needs to reject any such access.

To answer your main question: Yes, a C pointer on a 32-bit machine normally has 2^32 - 2 "valid" values, while a machine address has 2^32 - 1 valid ones. It's a small sacrifice to allow a pointer to signify a "points to nothing" state. The one single "invalid" value (machine address 0) can still be used if you know what you're doing.

Footnote: In reality, that whole NULL != 0 issue is more of a (useful) standardization rigmarole to rectify a historical "hack" to reserve machine address 0 for NULL. Originally, no one cared if you accessed NULL.

Q: HRNet trained from scratch on MPII high PCKh but poor visual predictions A:

I found the problem. It was not a training or model issue, but an inference coordinate reconstruction error.

The preprocessing steps applied during inference were:

  1. Detect person with YOLO (bounding box in original frame)

  2. Crop ROI

  3. Resize with aspect-ratio preservation

  4. Letterbox to 256×256

  5. Run HRNet

  6. Extract keypoints from heatmaps

The mistake was in the reverse mapping of keypoints to the original image. Key points were mapped back using a ratio-based scaling method, which assumed that the image would be resized directly. This method also ignored letterbox padding and non-uniform scaling. Because the preprocessing included a resize and padding that preserves the aspect ratio, the inverse transform must explicitly:

  1. Get rid of the padding offsets.

  2. Reset the scaling factor.

  3. Then move by the centre of the box.

If you don't do this, the keypoints will look wrong even if the predicted joint topology is correct.

If you use person cropping, aspect-ratio preserving resize, and letterboxing during inference, you must reverse these steps exactly. Otherwise, you might get the wrong idea from looking at the numbers.

Q: Can't connect a midi output device to .net MAUI using DryWetMidi A:

I'm the author of the DryWetMIDI. I've analyzed the problem:

  1. The bug is not with the library, it's a MAUI related one.
  2. The error comes from midiOutOpen system Windows function which fails for Microsoft GS Wavetable Synth in a MAUI project but works for any other project types.

I've reported the bug in MAUI repo: https://github.com/dotnet/maui/issues/12368. So what we have is to wait for response from Microsoft.

Update:

The bug has been moved to WinUI repo: https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-xaml/issues/8055. Also you can mark your project as Unpackaged and the issue should go away.
